prompt: What are the potential HR problems of using the “keeper test” as the basis for deciding whether to retain employees? Refer to the purposes, types and criteria of performance management.
modelAnswer: Purposes: the keeper test serves only accountability (keep or exit); development and communication are missing – no feedback on what to improve, no goal setting, so people do not know where they stand. Type: a single, holistic and subjective judgement by one manager, relative to an imagined replacement – close to a ranking without criteria. Criteria: low reliability (different managers, different standards, mood and recent events), questionable validity (what is “performance” – results, behaviours, potential? no job-related standards), prone to bias (similar-to-me, halo/horns, favouritism) and hard to defend legally; acceptability suffers because the threat of exit creates anxiety, risk aversion and politicking; individual focus may undermine collaboration in a culture that values teamwork; constant turnover is costly (severance, recruitment, lost knowledge) and can hurt diversity if “keepers” look like the manager.

prompt: Based on Cappelli & Tavis (2016), which business imperatives would push Netflix to abandon the keeper test? If Netflix keeps it, which other practices would be needed to make this appraisal effective?
modelAnswer: Imperatives: 1) People development – in a tight labour market for creative and technical talent, firing “adequate” performers instead of developing them is costly; employees want coaching. 2) Agility – fast-changing content and technology need frequent goal adjustment and feedback, not a binary keep/exit judgement. 3) Teamwork – productions and tech projects are team-based; a test about individuals can undermine cooperation and candour. If the test stays: clear, communicated expectations and criteria (what makes a keeper), frequent feedback and check-ins so nobody is surprised, development plans and a chance to improve before exit, calibration across managers and multiple sources of input (peers, 360°) to improve reliability and reduce bias, documentation and appeal, training of managers, separating development conversations from the keep/exit decision, and monitoring exits by group to detect bias.
keyPoints: Development, agility, teamwork applied to Netflix
Frequent feedback and development before exit

prompt: Why might a firm such as Netflix embrace inclusivity and diversity as a central part of its culture? Refer to the theoretical concepts studied in class.
modelAnswer: Business case: diverse teams bring different perspectives and innovate more – ethnic diversity especially drives radical innovation and cannot be substituted by external collaboration; this fits a creative company producing content for a global, diverse audience (market knowledge, authentic stories, global expansion). Better decisions: differing perspectives reduce groupthink, consistent with candour and independent decision-making. Talent: an inclusive employer brand attracts the best people worldwide in a competitive labour market. Fighting bias: focusing on talent instead of similarity counters similar-to-me bias and “cultural fit” judged as “like us”, which would otherwise reproduce homogeneity. Sustainable HRM: instrumental (strategy, talent, investors) and values-driven reasons; social dimension of the triple bottom line. Link to the keeper test: inclusion norms are a safeguard so that subjective keep/exit judgements do not discriminate.
keyPoints: Reduces similar-to-me bias / cultural fit trap

prompt: Netflix links pay explicitly to the labour market: an employee's salary is set at what comparable employees with the same skills earn at peer firms (top of their personal market). What are the advantages and disadvantages of this reward strategy?
modelAnswer: This is a strong choice for external competitiveness (market pricing) over internal consistency. Advantages: attracts and retains top talent – no reason to leave for more money (lower quits, fits the dream-team logic); simple and transparent rationale; flexible for scarce skills; supports a high-performance employer brand; equity theory – employees compare with outside referents and feel fairly paid. Disadvantages: very expensive; market data are hard to obtain and estimate (subjective “personal market”); internal inconsistency – people in similar roles may earn very different pay, causing perceived inequity with internal referents; pay follows the market, not the value of the job or contribution, and can fall when the market drops; may attract people motivated mainly by money (extrinsic) and crowd out commitment; can reproduce market inequalities (e.g. gender pay gaps embedded in market rates); little variable pay means weak line of sight between performance and pay, although annual recalibration includes performance.
keyPoints: Cost and difficulty of market data
Market can embed inequality; extrinsic motivation
